artifacts.title: Hospital Discharge Summary - Anterior STEMI s/p PCI
artifacts.author: Inpatient Cardiology Service
artifacts.body:
55-year-old male presented with acute anterior STEMI. Emergent cardiac catheterization revealed 100% occlusion of the proximal LAD. Successful PCI with placement of one drug-eluting stent. Peak troponin 42 ng/mL. Transthoracic echocardiogram day 3: LVEF 40%, anteroapical hypokinesis, no thrombus. Hospital course uncomplicated. Discharged home in stable condition.

Discharge medications: Aspirin 81 mg daily (indefinite), Ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily (minimum 12 months - explicit counseling given on risk of stent thrombosis with early discontinuation, including risk of death or recurrent MI), Atorvastatin 80 mg nightly, Metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, Lisinopril 5 mg daily.

Referrals placed: Outpatient cardiac rehabilitation, follow-up with primary cardiologist in 4-6 weeks, primary care follow-up in 1-2 weeks.

Counseling provided on smoking cessation (patient was abstinent during admission), diet, and activity restrictions (no heavy lifting x 2 weeks, gradual return to activity).

artifacts.title: Active Medication List - Pharmacy Fill History
artifacts.author: Retail Pharmacy Records

artifacts.title: Transthoracic Echocardiogram - Day 3 Post-MI
artifacts.author: Echocardiography Lab
artifacts.body:
LEFT VENTRICLE: Mild-moderately reduced systolic function, LVEF 40% (biplane Simpson's method). Regional wall motion abnormality: akinesis of distal anteroseptal and apical segments, hypokinesis of mid-anterior segment, consistent with LAD territory infarct. No LV thrombus identified.

RIGHT VENTRICLE: Normal size and systolic function.

VALVES: Trace to mild mitral regurgitation. Aortic and tricuspid valves structurally normal. No significant stenosis or regurgitation otherwise.

ATRIA: Normal size.

PERICARDIUM: No effusion.

IMPRESSION: Reduced LVEF 40% with anteroapical wall motion abnormality consistent with recent anterior MI. No thrombus. Recommend repeat echo in 3-6 months to reassess for recovery of function and consideration of ICD if EF remains ≤35% on GDMT.

artifacts.title: Prior Office Visit Note - 2 Weeks Post-Discharge (Primary Care)
artifacts.author: Primary Care Physician
artifacts.body: Patient seen for post-discharge follow-up. Reports doing 'okay', denies chest pain. States he is taking his medications. Incision sites healing well. Advised to continue cardiology follow-up and start cardiac rehab. Did not screen for mood symptoms at this visit. Blood pressure 128/80, HR 72. Discussed importance of smoking cessation; patient reported he had not smoked since the hospital stay (reported at that time, prior to relapse).

objectives.text: Elicit and reconcile adherence to dual antiplatelet therapy, recognizing the discrepancy between patient's self-report and pharmacy refill data, and counsel on the risk of stent thrombosis from premature ticagrelor discontinuation.
Screen for and identify post-MI depression and sexual/activity-related fear using validated tools and sensitive direct questioning, going beyond the patient's deflecting humor.
Assess cardiac rehabilitation engagement and barriers (cost, time, transportation, work demands) and formulate a plan to re-engage the patient.
Integrate echocardiogram, lipid panel, and risk-factor data (smoking relapse, LDL above goal, reduced work-life balance) into a guideline-directed secondary prevention plan.
Perform a remote cardiovascular exam appropriate to telehealth (camera-guided JVP, self-palpation for edema, exertional oximetry) to screen for heart failure decompensation.

Recognize when findings (persistent LVEF 40%, ongoing symptoms) require referral back to the primary interventional/device team or electrophysiology rather than independent management by this role alone, respecting scope of practice.

mismatches.patientClaim: I'm taking everything, all five pills, every single day, doc.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy fill history shows ticagrelor 90mg was filled once at discharge (30-day supply) with zero refills since; last fill was 5 weeks ago, while the other four medications have been refilled on schedule.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-reported adherence is often inaccurate, especially for costly or side-effect-prone medications; objective pharmacy/refill data should be cross-checked, particularly for drugs with high consequences of discontinuation like P2Y12 inhibitors after recent stent placement.

mismatches.patientClaim: I think I'm signed up for the rehab thing, they're supposed to call me.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Cardiac rehab program records show the referral was received but no intake appointment was ever scheduled and the patient has attended zero sessions, despite two voicemails left by the program.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Passive referral without active follow-up often fails; patients may believe they are 'enrolled' when no concrete appointment exists, highlighting the need for closed-loop referral tracking in post-MI care.

facts.chart: Presents for scheduled 6-week post-MI cardiology follow-up after anterior STEMI with PCI/DES to LAD.
facts.says: I'm here for my check-up after the heart attack back in the spring. Doc said six weeks and here I am.

facts.chart: Denies current chest pain, pressure, or tightness at rest or with exertion.
facts.says: No chest pain, nothing like what I had before. Thank God.

facts.chart: Reports mild breathlessness with exertion such as climbing stairs or standing at the stove for long periods, no breathlessness at rest.
facts.says: I get a little winded going up the stairs at the restaurant, more than before. Lying down I'm fine though.

facts.chart: Denies leg swelling, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.
facts.says: No swelling in my ankles, and I sleep fine, don't wake up gasping or anything.

facts.chart: Denies palpitations, presyncope, or syncope since discharge.
facts.says: No, my heart doesn't do anything funny that I notice. No fainting.

facts.chart: States he is taking all five discharge medications as prescribed, including the twice-daily antiplatelet.
facts.says: I'm taking everything, all five pills, every single day, doc.

facts.chart: Reports taking ticagrelor as prescribed when asked specifically; later, with direct questioning about side effects, admits he stopped it 12 days ago.
facts.says: The one for the stent? Yeah, I take that too... well, I mean, I did take it.

facts.chart: Discontinued ticagrelor 12 days ago due to subjective breathlessness attributed to the medication and difficulty affording the copay.
facts.says: It made me feel short of breath, like I couldn't catch my air, and honestly the copay for that one pill is almost $150 a month. The others are cheap, that one's not.

facts.chart: Aware that his heart's pumping function was reduced after the heart attack per discharge discussion; unsure of current status.
facts.says: They told me my heart's pump is weaker now, something like 40 percent. I don't really know what that means for me now.

facts.chart: History of anterior ST-elevation MI 6 weeks ago, treated with primary PCI and drug-eluting stent to the LAD.
facts.says: I had the big one, the heart attack, back in the spring. They put a stent in.

facts.chart: No prior history of MI, heart failure, or arrhythmia before this event.
facts.says: Never had any heart trouble before this, I was always healthy, or so I thought.

facts.chart: No history of diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or prior stroke.
facts.says: No diabetes, no kidney problems, never had a stroke.

facts.chart: Sleeps on one pillow, no need to prop up to breathe.
facts.says: I sleep flat, same as always, don't need extra pillows.

facts.chart: Able to walk about 2 blocks or one flight of stairs before needing to pause, worse than pre-MI baseline of unlimited activity.
facts.says: I used to run up and down those stairs all day at the restaurant, now I gotta stop partway up sometimes.

facts.chart: Denies abdominal bloating, early satiety, or weight gain suggestive of fluid retention; reports stable weight.
facts.says: My pants fit the same, no bloating, nothing like that.

facts.chart: Endorses low mood, decreased interest in activities, and fatigue most days since the MI, using humor to deflect from the topic initially.
facts.says: Mood? Ha, I'm Greek, we don't do moods, we do coffee and complaining. But yeah... I've been a little down, I guess.

facts.chart: Reports feeling 'useless' and like a burden to his family some days since the cardiac event.
facts.says: Some days I just feel useless, like I'm no good to anybody, sitting around instead of working.

facts.chart: Denies any thoughts of self-harm or suicide when asked directly.
facts.says: No, no, nothing like that. I would never do that to my wife and kids.

facts.chart: Reports avoiding sexual activity with spouse since the MI due to fear of triggering another cardiac event; has not discussed this fear with any provider until now.
facts.says: Me and my wife... we haven't been close like that since this happened. I'm scared something's gonna happen, you know, during. I never told anybody this.

facts.chart: Expresses significant fear of exertion in general, worried that physical activity could trigger another heart attack, contributing to deconditioning avoidance.
facts.says: Every time I feel my heart beating a little fast I think, is this it, is this another one.

facts.chart: Has not attended any cardiac rehabilitation sessions since the referral was placed at discharge 6 weeks ago.
facts.says: The rehab thing... I haven't gone yet, honestly. Been meaning to.

facts.chart: Cites 14-hour workdays running his restaurant and lack of time as the main barrier to attending cardiac rehab sessions.
facts.says: I'm at the restaurant like 14 hours a day, who's gonna run the place if I'm not there? I don't have time for classes.

facts.chart: Believes he is enrolled in cardiac rehab and waiting for the program to contact him with a start date.
facts.says: I think I'm signed up for the rehab thing, they're supposed to call me.

facts.chart: Resumed smoking approximately 3 weeks ago after being abstinent during hospitalization; initially minimizes amount.
facts.says: I had a couple cigarettes here and there, just a few, nothing like before.

facts.chart: Currently smoking approximately half a pack (10 cigarettes) per day for the past 3 weeks, stress-related relapse tied to work and worry.
facts.says: Okay, fine, it's more like half a pack a day now. The restaurant stress, the worry about money... it gets to me.

facts.chart: Returned to working approximately 14-hour days at his restaurant within 3-4 weeks of discharge, against general activity-pacing advice.
facts.says: I'm back to full days at the restaurant, 14 hours, same as always. Business doesn't stop for a heart attack.

facts.chart: Reports attempting to reduce salt and fried foods but acknowledges difficulty given his restaurant's menu and long hours around food all day.
facts.says: I'm trying to eat better, less salt, less fried stuff, but I'm surrounded by food all day at work, it's hard.

facts.chart: Father died of a heart attack at age 58; one brother with hypertension.
facts.says: My dad died of a heart attack at 58. My brother's got high blood pressure.

facts.chart: Lives with wife and two adult children; wife is primary source of emotional support but unaware of extent of his fears and medication nonadherence.
facts.says: I live with my wife, kids are grown but still around. My wife worries about me but I don't tell her everything.

facts.chart: Drinks 1-2 glasses of wine on weekends, no change since the MI, no history of heavy alcohol use.
facts.says: Little wine on Sundays with family, that's it, always been that way.

facts.chart: Reports a brief weekend trip to visit relatives in Michigan 2 weeks ago, no symptoms during travel, no prolonged immobility.
facts.says: We drove up to see family in Michigan a couple weeks ago for a weekend, I was fine the whole time.

facts.chart: No known drug allergies.
facts.says: No allergies to any medicines that I know of.

facts.chart: Denies fever, chills, or recent infections.
facts.says: No fevers, I haven't been sick or anything.

facts.chart: Primary goal is to get reassurance that he is 'cleared' to return fully to normal life and work without restrictions.
facts.says: I just want you to tell me I'm good to go, back to normal, no more worrying.

patient.name: Dennis Papadakis
patient.appearance: A stocky, broad-shouldered man with graying dark hair and a thick mustache, appearing his age, seated at a small desk in a cluttered back office that looks like it is part of a restaurant, with a menu board visible behind him. He wears a short-sleeved collared shirt with the restaurant's logo, leans back with arms crossed at times, and alternates between a joking grin and a tired, guarded expression.

persona.personality: Warm, proud, and quick with humor as a deflection; a hardworking small-business owner who sees himself as the strong provider for his family and is uncomfortable appearing weak or dependent.
persona.communicationStyle: Talks in an animated, informal way, often cracking jokes or changing the subject when conversations turn toward feelings, fear, or money; responds well to direct, respectful questions once rapport builds.
persona.emotionalState: Outwardly jovial but underneath anxious about his health, finances, and his ability to keep running the restaurant; minimizes distress until pressed gently and persistently.
persona.background: Immigrated with his parents from Greece as a child, took over the family restaurant from his father 20 years ago, works long hours alongside his wife and occasionally his adult children, prides himself on never having called in sick before this year.
speechExamples: Doc, I feel like a million bucks, well, maybe eight hundred thousand.
You want me to sit still for a cardiac rehab class? I got a restaurant to run!
My wife, she worries too much, I tell her I'm fine, fine like Greek yogurt, extra thick.
Honestly? That pill was costing me more than my gas bill.
I don't like talking about this stuff, but... okay, doc, I'll tell you.
concerns: Wants to be told he can go back to full normal activity without restrictions
Worried about the cost of his medications, especially the expensive one
Embarrassed to discuss mood, fear, and intimacy issues, hides behind jokes
Fears that any symptom (fast heartbeat, breathlessness) means another heart attack is imminent
Worried about who will run the restaurant if he has to slow down

scenario.studentBrief: You are the cardiology fellow conducting a telehealth follow-up visit with Dennis Papadakis, a 55-year-old man who had an anterior STEMI treated with primary PCI and a drug-eluting stent to the LAD six weeks ago. He was discharged on dual antiplatelet therapy, a statin, a beta-blocker, and an ACE inhibitor, with a discharge echocardiogram showing LVEF 40%. He is calling from his restaurant for a scheduled post-MI follow-up visit.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Six-week post-MI follow-up after anterior STEMI with PCI/DES to LAD.
scenario.openingLine: Hey doc, good to see you. I'm here for my check-up after the heart attack back in the spring, six weeks like you said.
tasks: Take a focused history of cardiac and functional status since discharge, including a remote cardiovascular exam appropriate to telehealth.
Reconcile the patient's reported medication adherence against objective pharmacy records and address any gaps, particularly dual antiplatelet therapy.
Screen for post-MI depression, anxiety about activity/intimacy, and assess cardiac rehabilitation engagement and barriers.
Review and integrate the discharge echocardiogram, current lipid panel, and risk-factor status (smoking, work hours) into a secondary prevention and guideline-directed therapy plan.
Determine whether any findings require referral back to the interventional/device or primary care team, and document a consult note (SOAP) with clear next steps.

profile.summary: A 55-year-old restaurant owner presents for routine 6-week follow-up after an anterior STEMI treated with PCI/DES to the LAD, discharged with LVEF 40% on guideline-directed therapy. Beneath an upbeat exterior, he has secretly stopped ticagrelor 12 days ago due to side effects and cost, has not attended cardiac rehabilitation, resumed smoking at half a pack per day, returned to 14-hour workdays, and is hiding depressive symptoms and fear-driven avoidance of exertion and intimacy. The case teaches fellows to reconcile self-reported adherence against objective pharmacy data, screen sensitively for psychosocial sequelae of MI, and build a secondary-prevention plan while recognizing when to loop in primary care, rehab, and the device/interventional team rather than managing everything in isolation.
profile.title: Six-Week Post-STEMI Follow-Up: The Patient Who 'Takes Everything'
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient at a small desk in the back office of his restaurant in Chicago

answerKey.primaryProblem: Premature discontinuation of ticagrelor (dual antiplatelet therapy) 12 days after an anterior STEMI with DES to the LAD, placing the patient at high risk for stent thrombosis, compounded by unaddressed post-MI depression, smoking relapse, non-engagement with cardiac rehabilitation, and LDL above goal.
differential: Stent thrombosis risk from premature P2Y12 inhibitor discontinuation (most urgent concern)
Post-MI major depressive episode with associated anxiety and avoidance behaviors (exertional and sexual)
Residual/ongoing LV systolic dysfunction (LVEF 40%) with possible mild exertional dyspnea from deconditioning versus early heart failure
Medication cost/access barrier as a root cause of nonadherence rather than simple noncompliance
Tobacco use relapse as an independent major modifiable cardiovascular risk factor
LDL above secondary-prevention goal despite high-intensity statin, raising question of adherence versus need for additional lipid-lowering therapy (e.g., ezetimibe/PCSK9 inhibitor)
keyFindings: Patient reports full medication adherence, but pharmacy records show ticagrelor was filled only once at discharge with no refill in 5 weeks
Patient admits, only when asked directly and after rapport-building, that he stopped ticagrelor 12 days ago due to perceived breathlessness and the ~$150/month copay
LVEF 40% with anteroapical hypokinesis on discharge echo, no thrombus, mild MR
LDL 96 mg/dL on current high-intensity statin, above the <70 mg/dL goal for very-high-risk secondary prevention
PHQ-9 score 13 (moderate depression); denies active suicidal ideation
Zero cardiac rehab sessions attended despite believing he is 'signed up'; patient unaware intake was never scheduled
Smoking relapse to approximately half a pack/day for 3 weeks, initially minimized
Hidden fear of exertion and avoidance of sexual intimacy since the MI, disclosed only with direct, sensitive questioning
Mild exertional desaturation (96% to 94%) with 1 minute marching in place, correlating with his reported stair-climbing limitation
plan: Urgently reinitiate ticagrelor 90mg twice daily today given high risk of stent thrombosis within the first year after DES placement, especially this early; discuss cost-mitigation options (manufacturer patient assistance program, pharmacy cost-comparison, or discuss alternative P2Y12 inhibitor such as clopidogrel with the original PCI operator if cost remains prohibitive) and ensure a bridge supply is obtained before the current visit ends
Communicate urgently with the interventional cardiologist/PCI operator regarding the 12-day DAPT gap to coordinate shared decision-making on P2Y12 inhibitor choice and any need for closer monitoring
Address LDL above goal: reinforce atorvastatin 80mg adherence, discuss adding ezetimibe if LDL remains >70 mg/dL at next recheck in 4-6 weeks

Refer/re-engage with mental health: provide warm handoff or referral to behavioral health/psychiatry for further evaluation and treatment of moderate depressive symptoms; screen again for suicidality at next contact

Address sexual health concerns: reassure that resuming sexual activity is generally safe at this point post-MI without ongoing anginal symptoms, but formally loop in primary care or request a symptom-limited exercise stress test if any uncertainty about functional capacity before clearing for exertion-equivalent activity
Reconnect proactively with cardiac rehabilitation program; discuss flexible scheduling or home-based/hybrid cardiac rehab options given his 14-hour workdays as a barrier
Smoking cessation counseling and referral to a tobacco cessation program or pharmacotherapy (e.g., varenicline or nicotine replacement), tailored to relapse triggers (work stress)
Counsel on activity pacing and realistic return-to-work expectations; recommend reducing to a more sustainable schedule if feasible, with gradual increase in activity under cardiac rehab guidance
Schedule repeat echocardiogram in 3-6 months per discharge echo recommendation to reassess EF for possible ICD consideration if EF remains ≤35% on GDMT
Loop in primary care physician regarding depression screen results and medication reconciliation findings for continuity of care
redFlags: 12-day gap in dual antiplatelet therapy after DES to LAD within the first 6 weeks post-PCI, a critical window for stent thrombosis risk
Moderate depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 13) with feelings of being 'useless' and a burden, requiring suicide risk screening and ongoing monitoring even though currently denies active ideation
Mild exertional desaturation and reduced activity tolerance in the setting of LVEF 40%, warranting ongoing surveillance for heart failure decompensation versus deconditioning
educationPoints: Self-reported medication adherence frequently overestimates true adherence; objective data (pharmacy refill history, prescription claims) should be routinely cross-checked, especially for high-stakes medications like P2Y12 inhibitors after recent stenting

Cost and side effects are common, under-disclosed reasons for stopping cardioprotective medications; proactively asking about affordability and side effects can uncover nonadherence that direct 'are you taking your medications' questions miss

Depression, anxiety, and sexual dysfunction are common and underreported after MI; validated screening tools (e.g., PHQ-9) and direct, nonjudgmental questions are necessary since patients often minimize or joke about these symptoms

Passive referral to cardiac rehabilitation without active follow-up frequently results in nonattendance; closed-loop referral processes and addressing concrete barriers (time, cost, scheduling) improve engagement

LDL goals after MI are more stringent (<70 mg/dL, often <55 mg/dL for very-high-risk patients) than general primary prevention goals, and adherence plus add-on therapy should be considered when goals are not met on statin alone

Telehealth cardiovascular exams have real limitations (e.g., JVP assessment is often unreliable by camera) and should be supplemented with functional surrogates like home oximetry during exertion and self-reported activity tolerance

When findings raise concerns beyond this role's primary scope (e.g., DAPT regimen changes affecting stent choice, cardiac rehab logistics, mental health treatment), timely communication and referral to the appropriate team member is essential rather than managing everything unilaterally
